title: The sandbox image

story: Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, claims a fresh VM for RH-1234, and the clock starts. The frontend's npm ci takes four minutes. Playwright's browser is another minute. FCP Lab, the full product running on the VM with fake data, has to build its images and seed its database, which takes twenty more. On a ticket whose real work is a small empty-state card, most of the run would be spent downloading the same files every other run downloads.

So all of that is done once a night, into the machine image every VM starts from. But the night is long. By the afternoon main has moved: someone added a package, the lockfile changed, and a VM that trusts last night's node_modules runs its tests against the wrong packages.
hook.question: How do we bake the slow, identical work into the image, and still know at claim time exactly what has changed since the bake?

p: Every sandbox VM starts from one machine image, ai-agent-sandbox, built every night with Packer and Ansible (the image lesson shows how). The rule for what goes in is simple: anything that is slow and the same for every run. That is the toolchain (Docker, Node 24, Python 3.13 with uv, git), a git mirror of the fcp repo, the npm and uv caches with node_modules already installed, Playwright's Chromium, FCP Lab with its images built and its fake data seeded, a pinned Claude Code, our plugins, and the harness, our program that runs the Claude session on the VM, unpacked from its release file.

Anything that differs per run stays out: the ticket, the branch, the run's capability for the broker (the service that holds our GitHub, Jira and Slack keys) and the token for the LLM gateway (the service that adds our Anthropic key to model calls). Those are written onto the VM at claim time and die with the run. No key of any kind is baked in.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the host rules in the image
p: The image also decides what the agent's user can do. The harness runs as a non-root user, agent, but that user is in the docker group, and anyone who can run containers can become root on the machine. So we assume a fooled agent can reach root, and the instance role holds almost nothing worth stealing. An iptables rule still lets only root, which runs the SSM agent, reach the instance metadata address, and a second rule drops it for containers.

Two small things complete the base: a spot-watch timer that writes a file when AWS announces it will take a Spot machine back, and unattended upgrades turned off, because the image is rebuilt every night instead of changing on its own.

read.h: The manifest: write down what you baked
p: Baking only works if the run can tell what is stale. So the last step of the bake writes a manifest, a small JSON file at /etc/ai-agent-sandbox/manifest.json, with the facts a run needs to compare: the commit of the fcp mirror, the SHA-256 hash of every lockfile that was installed, and the versions of FCP Lab, Claude Code and the harness. A hash is a fingerprint of a file's contents: the same file always gives the same hash, and any change gives a different one.
The Dockerfile below plays the image build in the lab. It installs once, then writes the hash of the lockfile it installed from.

code.file: Dockerfile (the lab's stand-in for the nightly bake)
code.text:
FROM node:24-bookworm-slim
WORKDIR /work/app
COPY app/package.json app/package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --no-audit --no-fund
RUN mkdir -p /etc/ai-agent-sandbox && \
    echo "{\"bakedAt\":\"$(date -u +%FT%TZ)\",\"lockSha\":\"$(sha256sum package-lock.json | cut -d' ' -f1)\"}" \
      > /etc/ai-agent-sandbox/manifest.json
COPY freshen.sh /usr/local/bin/freshen
RUN chmod 0755 /usr/local/bin/freshen

notes.text: The slow part, done once at bake time.
The manifest records the hash of the exact lockfile that node_modules was installed from.
The freshen step, which runs when a run claims the VM.

p: When a run claims a VM, a step called freshen brings it to the exact commit the run needs. It fetches that commit through the broker and checks it out, which is fast because the mirror already has almost every object. Then it hashes each lockfile again and compares it with the manifest. If a hash matches, node_modules is still right and nothing is installed. If it differs, that one install runs again, npm ci in frontend/ or uv sync in cloud/ and client/, with packages from our mirrors. On the bigger VMs FCP Lab is refreshed to the new code the same way, and only rebuilt when it says it must be.

This is what makes a run start in minutes: the image is right for most of the code, and the manifest says precisely where it is not. It also makes a failure easier to read, because a VM that was freshened against main's commit has a known-good starting point.

code.file: freshen.sh (the lab's version, for one lockfile)
code.text:
#!/bin/sh
# Run at claim time: redo only what changed since the image was baked.
set -e
cd /work/app
baked=$(node -p 'require("/etc/ai-agent-sandbox/manifest.json").lockSha')
now=$(sha256sum package-lock.json | cut -d' ' -f1)
if [ "$baked" = "$now" ]; then
  echo "lockfile unchanged since the bake: keeping node_modules"
else
  echo "lockfile changed (baked ${baked%"${baked#????????}"}, now ${now%"${now#????????}"}): npm ci"
  npm ci --no-audit --no-fund
fi

notes.text: What the bake installed from, read from the manifest.
What this run needs, hashed now.
Same hash, same packages: skip the slow step.
Different hash: reinstall exactly this part, nothing else.

read.see:
$ freshen   (same lockfile as the bake)
lockfile unchanged since the bake: keeping node_modules
$ freshen   (after someone added left-pad)
lockfile changed (baked 1d771b37, now 6d060725): npm ci
added 2 packages in 172ms

deeper.h: Go deeper: the mirror, and proving the image every night
p: The fcp checkout is made with git clone --reference from the baked mirror, so it borrows objects instead of downloading them. A clone like that still has the mirror as its origin, so freshen must point origin at the broker's git address before it fetches, or the fetch would read last night's mirror and nothing newer.

A broken image would break every run at once, so a new image is never used before it passed a smoke test. Each night a workflow builds it on a testing channel, boots one VM from it, checks that the harness starts and runs one end-to-end test in FCP Lab, and always terminates that VM. Only then is the image's ID written to the parameter every launch template reads, with the previous ID kept next to it, so a rollback is one write.

lab.title: Bake once, freshen the difference
needs: Node and npm on your laptop, and internet for two small packages
lab.goal: Bake an image that installs packages once and records the lockfile's hash, then show that freshen skips the install when nothing changed and redoes it when the lockfile moved.

guess.q: The image was baked last night from lockfile A. Today the run's commit has lockfile B, with one new package. What should freshen do?

options.text: Nothing, because node_modules is already in the image.
options.why: Those are lockfile A's packages. Tests would run against the wrong set, and the failure would look like a code bug.

options.text: Reinstall that one part, because the lockfile's hash no longer matches the manifest.
options.why: The manifest exists for exactly this comparison: same hash, skip; different hash, redo only that install.

options.text: Throw the VM away and wait for tonight's image.
options.why: Redoing one install takes seconds or minutes. Waiting a night for every lockfile change would stop all work.

lab.build: Our image installs from two kinds of lockfile: package-lock.json for the frontend and uv.lock for the backend. Give your bake a second, made-up lockfile, backend.lock (any text file), and record both hashes in the manifest under frontendLock and backendLock. Change freshen so it compares each one separately and prints which install it would redo, for example "backend: uv sync" (echo is enough for the backend). Show the three cases: nothing changed, only the frontend changed, only the backend changed.
checks: The manifest holds the hash of the lockfile the image was baked from.
With the same lockfile, freshen installs nothing and returns in well under a second.
With a changed lockfile, freshen runs npm ci and node_modules holds the new package.
With two lockfiles, changing one of them redoes only its own install.
You removed the image afterwards: docker rmi sandbox.

solution.text:
#!/bin/sh
set -e
cd /work/app
check() { # name, file, manifest field, command
  baked=$(node -p "require('/etc/ai-agent-sandbox/manifest.json').$3")
  now=$(sha256sum "$2" | cut -d' ' -f1)
  if [ "$baked" = "$now" ]; then echo "$1: unchanged"; else echo "$1: $4"; sh -c "$4"; fi
}
check frontend package-lock.json frontendLock "npm ci --no-audit --no-fund"
check backend backend.lock backendLock "echo uv sync would run here"

# In the Dockerfile, after COPY of both files:
# RUN echo "{\"frontendLock\":\"$(sha256sum package-lock.json | cut -d' ' -f1)\",\"backendLock\":\"$(sha256sum backend.lock | cut -d' ' -f1)\"}" > /etc/ai-agent-sandbox/manifest.json

lab.fix: A teammate wanted faster claims, so they changed freshen to compare the lockfile's modification time with bakedAt instead of its hash. Recreate it: a checkout writes every file with the time of the checkout, so the lockfile always looks newer, and every run reinstalls. Then try the opposite mistake: copy an old lockfile over with its time preserved (touch -d), and the changed packages are skipped. Put the hash comparison back and explain why a hash is the only honest answer to "is this the same file?".
explain: What decides whether something belongs in the image or is written at claim time?
What does the manifest record, and which step reads it?
Why does freshen compare hashes instead of trusting that last night's node_modules is close enough?
lab.done: Your image skips the install when the lockfile matches the manifest and redoes exactly the install whose lockfile changed.

check.q: Which of these belongs in the nightly image?

options.text: The run's broker capability, so the harness can start faster
options.why: It is different for every run and dies with the run. It is written at claim time, never baked.

options.text: FCP Lab with its images built and fake data seeded
options.why: It is slow and the same for every run, which is exactly what baking is for.

options.text: A GitHub token for cloning fcp at run time
options.why: No key is ever baked in. At run time git goes through the broker, which holds the token.

check.q: The manifest says the frontend lockfile hash is 1d771b37…, and the run's commit has the same hash. What does freshen do for the frontend?

options.text: Runs npm ci anyway, to be safe
options.why: That throws away the whole point of baking. The same hash means the same packages.

options.text: Deletes node_modules and waits for the next image
options.why: Nothing is wrong with them; they match the lockfile exactly.
Same hash, same file, same packages. Only a changed lockfile triggers its own install.

check.q: Why does the bake record lockfile hashes instead of letting each run check node_modules with npm ls?

options.text: A hash comparison is one fast, exact question; the manifest also covers uv, FCP Lab and tool versions the same way
options.why: One file answers "what did we bake?" for every part, and a hash answers "is it the same?" without guessing.
npm ls works offline. The reason is speed and one uniform check, not network.
Packer does not care. The manifest is our own design for the claim step.

p: The image is packer/images/ai-agent-sandbox with the Ansible role ai_agent_sandbox, built from rhino-base-ubuntu-24 on m8i.2xlarge with a 120 GB disk: Docker CE, Node 24 (fcp's frontend needs 24.15 or newer), Python 3.13 and uv, git and jq, no gh CLI, the agent user (uid 1001, in the docker group), the IMDS iptables rules, spot-watch every 5 seconds and unattended upgrades off. One image serves lite, full and wide; the size is the instance type. The AMI is shared with the ai-agents account through infrastructure PR #1724.

The heavy bake adds the bare mirror /var/cache/git/fcp.git (cloned with a short-lived build token that is never written to disk), /work/fcp via --reference, npm ci and Playwright Chromium in frontend/, uv sync in cloud/ and client/, FCP Lab at a pinned tag (lab up, status ready, lab stop), Claude Code pinned under /usr/local with updates off, /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json, our plugins at a pinned ref, nova-worker from its release tarball, and /etc/ai-agent-sandbox/manifest.json. build-ai-agent-sandbox.yml builds nightly on the testing channel, smoke-tests over SSM (nova-worker --version, then one FCP Lab e2e spec), promotes by writing /ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id and keeping ami-id-previous, and alerts #ai-agents-alerts on failure.

tickets.why: The base image: toolchain, the agent user, the metadata lock, spot-watch, upgrades off.
The heavy bake: fcp mirror, caches, Chromium, FCP Lab, Claude Code, plugins, the harness and the manifest.
The nightly build with a smoke test, promotion through the SSM parameter, and one-write rollback.
freshen reads the manifest at claim time and redoes only what changed.

words.plain: Do slow setup once, while building the machine image, instead of on every VM.
A small JSON file the bake writes, recording what it installed: commits, lockfile hashes, versions.
A fingerprint of a file's contents: the same file always gives the same hash, any change gives another.
The claim-time step that brings a VM to the run's commit and redoes only the installs whose lockfile changed.

review.q: Name four things the image bakes and two things it must never contain.
review.a: Baked: toolchain, fcp mirror, npm and uv caches with node_modules, Chromium, FCP Lab with fake data, Claude Code, plugins, the harness, the manifest. Never: any key or token, and anything specific to one run.

review.q: Main's backend lockfile changed at noon. Describe what a run claimed at 14:00 does before Nova starts.
review.a: freshen fetches the run's commit through the broker, compares each lockfile hash with the manifest, sees the backend one differs, runs uv sync in cloud/ and client/ from our mirror, keeps the frontend as baked, refreshes FCP Lab if needed, and checks the lab is ready.

remember: Bake whatever is slow and the same for every run, write down what you baked, and at claim time redo only what the manifest says has changed.
